records.title: StackOverflowError: unbounded mutual recursion between the argument→select and select→argument steps in ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment
records.body:
### What version of OpenRewrite are you using?

Reproduced against `org.openrewrite.meta:rewrite-analysis:2.38.0-SNAPSHOT` (the stack trace line numbers below match that build exactly).

### How are you running OpenRewrite?

Via `org.openrewrite.staticanalysis.ReplaceStackWithDeque`, which uses `FindLocalFlowPaths` with a plain `DataFlowSpec`.

### What is the smallest, simplest way to reproduce the problem?

```java
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.Stack;

class Test {
    void test(Optional<String> opt) {
        Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();
        String a = "x";
        String s = Optional.ofNullable(a).orElse(opt.get());
    }
}
```

(The `Stack` is only there to satisfy the recipe's `UsesType` precondition; the overflow happens while computing flow out of `a`.)

### What did you expect to see?

The recipe completes.

### What did you see instead?

`java.lang.StackOverflowError`, with ~1000 frames alternating between exactly two call sites in `ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment`:

```
java.lang.StackOverflowError
  ...
  org.openrewrite.Cursor.getParentTreeCursor(Cursor.java:253)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.expr.VarAccessBase.viewOf(VarAccess.java:221)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.expr.VarAccess$Factory.viewOf(VarAccess.java:86)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.TraitFactory.findFirstViewOf(TraitFactory.java:87)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.TraitFactory.lambda$findFirstViewOf$2(TraitFactory.java:96)
  fj.data.Validation$FailProjection.bind(Validation.java:1249)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.TraitFactory.findFirstViewOf(TraitFactory.java:95)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.TraitFactory.findFirstViewOf(TraitFactory.java:69)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.expr.Expr$Factory.viewOf(Expr.java:37)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.trait.expr.Expr.viewOf(Expr.java:51)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.dataflow.DataFlowNode.of(DataFlowNode.java:63)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.dataflow.analysis.ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment(ForwardFlow.java:458)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.dataflow.analysis.ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment(ForwardFlow.java:495)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.dataflow.analysis.ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment(ForwardFlow.java:466)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.dataflow.analysis.ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment(ForwardFlow.java:495)
  org.openrewrite.analysis.dataflow.analysis.ForwardFlow.computeVariableAssignment(ForwardFlow.java:466)
  ... (502 frames at :466, 501 frames at :495)
```

### Root cause

`computeVariableAssignment` has two mutually recursive descents into siblings of the *same* `J.MethodInvocation`, with no visited set and no depth bound:

- [`ForwardFlow.java:455-472`](https://github.com/openrewrite/rewrite-analysis/blob/main/src/main/java/org/openrewrite/analysis/dataflow/analysis/ForwardFlow.java#L455-L472) — "flow from an argument to the select", recursing on the **select** cursor (line 466).
- [`ForwardFlow.java:477-503`](https://github.com/openrewrite/rewrite-analysis/blob/main/src/main/java/org/openrewrite/analysis/dataflow/analysis/ForwardFlow.java#L477-L503) — "flow from the select (or another argument) to an argument", recursing on the **argument** cursor (line 495).

If `spec.isFlowStep(..)` holds in both directions for one call, the two branches call each other forever: `arg -> select -> arg -> select -> ...`.

For `Optional.ofNullable(a).orElse(opt.get())` both directions hold, and neither comes from a bidirectional model — they come from two *different* `ReturnValue` model groups that `Optimizer.optimize` merges into name-indexed union matchers:

- `flowFromArgumentIndexToReturn[0]` (models with `Argument[0] -> ReturnValue`, which includes `Optional.orElse` and `Optional.ofNullable`). Its predicate is `sinkNode is a Call matching M && isParameter(srcNode, 0)`. With src = `opt.get()` (argument 0 of `orElse`) and sink = `Optional.ofNullable(a)` (a `Call`, and `ofNullable` is in the group) this is a flow step — so the `arg -> select` branch fires.
- `flowFromArgumentIndexToReturn[-1]` (models with `Argument[this] -> ReturnValue`, which includes `Optional.orElse` and `Optional.get`). Its predicate is `sinkNode is a Call matching M && isSelect(srcNode)`. With src = `Optional.ofNullable(a)` (the select of `orElse`) and sink = `opt.get()` (a `Call`, and `get` is in the group) this is also a flow step — so the `select -> arg` branch fires.

So the trigger is: a call whose **select is itself a call** and whose **argument is itself a call**, where the outer method appears in both the `Argument[k] -> ReturnValue` and `Argument[this] -> ReturnValue` value-model groups. `Optional.orElse` is one such method; there are others.

The `forFlowFromArgumentIndexToQualifier` optimizer already asserts *"Argument[-1] is the 'select' or 'qualifier' of a method call. Flow would be cyclic."*, so the cycle hazard is known — it just isn't guarded on this path.

### Where this shows up in the wild

`org.openrewrite.staticanalysis.ReplaceStackWithDeque` on `spring-projects/spring-data-mongodb`, file
`spring-data-mongodb/src/main/java/org/springframework/data/mongodb/core/convert/MongoExampleMapper.java`.

Recurring since at least 2026-08-17 in the "Java best practices" and "Common static analysis issues" flagship runs on `dev`, against `ALL`, `Open Source`, `Netflix + Spring + Apache` and `Netflix + Spring`. Confirmed present in run `20260825041417-SSuzc` (`org.openrewrite.table.SourcesFileErrors` names `org.openrewrite.staticanalysis.ReplaceStackWithDeque` / `java.lang.StackOverflowError` with the trace above) and absent on 2026-08-26 — consistent with the trigger depending on which expressions in the file get full type attribution in a given LST build, not on anything about the `Stack` itself.

### Suggested fix

Guard the mutual recursion — e.g. carry a set of already-visited cursors (or the `FlowGraph` nodes already on the path) through `computeVariableAssignment` and skip a recursive descent into a node that is already on the curren

records.title: performance: pnpm 12 is slow for lockfile updates in large monorepos
records.body:
### Verify latest release

- [x] I verified that the issue exists in the latest pnpm release

### pnpm version

_No response_

### Which area(s) of pnpm are affected? (leave empty if unsure)

_No response_

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue or a replay of the bug

_No response_

### Reproduction steps

## Reproduction

The public reproduction is here: https://github.com/jamenh/pnpm-workspace-performance-reproduction

It contains:
- 6,833 workspace projects
- 87,630 internal `workspace:*` dependency edges

Clone the given repo above, then run

```sh
pnpm install --lockfile-only --frozen-lockfile --offline --reporter-ndjson
```

and 
```sh
yarn install --mode update-lockfile
```

Test on a warmed, non-noop scenario (e.g. updating a dependecy and update lockfile again) to test resolution time.

### Describe the Bug

## Summary

This is a follow-up to #14151. Our earlier reproduction did not isolate the relevant scaling factors well enough. But this issue does.

We are evaluating pnpm for a large monorepo migration from Yarn. We benchmarked `install` and `install --lockfile-only` and pnpm 12 beats Yarn on `install` by a lot but it is slower on `install --lockfile-only` . On this [representative reproduction](https://github.com/jamenh/pnpm-workspace-performance-reproduction), we are able to show that pnpm 12 is consistently slower than Yarn 4 for a lockfile-only update, and the gap grows as the repository scales. (This may not be a functional bug, we are filing this more as a performance issue since it isn't aligned with what's [advertized](https://github.com/pnpm/benchmarks/blob/main/benchmarks.md#lots-of-files). But feel free to redirect me to elsewhere.)

## Areas with clear optimization headroom
While investigating the reproduction, we found two areas that appear to have relatively direct optimization opportunities.

### Workspace discovery
Large monorepos contain many directories that are not workspaces, such as `examples/`, `stories/`, `fixtures/` and `tests/`. Recursive workspace patterns must traverse these directories, which makes workspace discovery slower.

We already use literal paths and one-level `parent/*` patterns wherever possible to avoid unnecessary recursive walks. However, pnpm currently still sends even these precise patterns through the generic wax glob walker. It also combines each pattern with every supported manifest name, repeating glob setup and directory work for every pattern.

We raised [PR #14262](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/14262) that explores fast paths for literal paths and one-level `parent/*` patterns to avoid the wax glob walker. On the reproduction, it reduces median workspace-scoping time from about 3.0 s to 0.84 s, a ~70% improvement.

### Workspace dependency resolution
In a large monorepo, many projects depend on the same internal workspace packages. pnpm repeats much of the same resolution work for each importer, which makes installs and lockfile updates slower as the workspace grows.

The resolver cache key includes [project_dir](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/ba1638da7e31dbda51982e35f375801d4a200d19/pnpm/crates/resolving-deps-resolver/src/resolve_dependency_tree/workspace_ctx.rs#L29-L100), which identifies the project that declares the dependency. Including it in the key basically prevents different projects from sharing the cached resolution.

We raised [PR #14266](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/14266) that separates the shared package resolution from the project-specific relative-link calculation. On the same reproduction, it reduces median resolution time from about 752 ms to 492 ms, improved ~35%.

## The ask
If these directions are sound, please leave comments/feedback on PRs and we would be happy to drive them to completion. But please feel free to take a different routes if you think it'll address the underlying problems better, it's fine these particular PRs don't land as long as the problems are addressed. Our priority is being able to migrate(we can't when our Yarn 4 baseline still beats pnpm 12 on lockfile update).

### Expected Behavior

Faster lockfile update.

### Which Node.js version are you using?

24.11.1

### Which operating systems have you used?

- [x] macOS
- [ ] Windows
- [ ] Linux

### If your OS is a Linux based, which one it is? (Include the version if relevant)

_No response_

records.title: [Feature] Cross-repository test impact analysis for workspaces"
records.body:
## Problem

Currently, when I make a change in a provider repository (e.g., a backend API), I have no way to know which tests in *consumer* repositories actually cover that change across the workspace.

The workspace feature already provides:
- Contract maps (which endpoints/services are provided/consumed)
- Blast radius (structural dependents across repos)
- Breaking change detection (contract diffs)

But there's a missing piece: **test impact**. If I change `backend-api/src/api/users.py`, I have to manually:
1. Run `repowise workspace blast-radius` to see which repos consume it
2. `cd` into each consumer repo
3. Run `repowise impacted-tests` in each one
4. Aggregate the results myself

This is tedious, error-prone, and defeats the purpose of having a unified workspace view. The whole point of workspace intelligence is answering cross-repo questions in one place.

## Proposed Solution

Add a new workspace command (and matching MCP tool / REST endpoint) that answers:

> "Given a change in provider repo X, which specific test files in consumer repos Y, Z should I run?"

The implementation would:
1. Take changed files in provider repos as input (e.g., `backend-api:src/api/users.py`)
2. Look up contract links from `contracts.json` to find consumer repos + call sites
3. For each consumer repo, query its test reachability index (call-graph 3-hop + import-graph fallback)
4. Return a unified list of test files across all consumer repos, tagged with:
   - **basis**: `measured` (per-test coverage) vs `inferred` (call/import graph)
   - **via**: `coverage-map` | `call-graph` | `import-graph`
   - **confidence**: from the contract link match
   - **source files**: which provider files this test ultimately reaches

Output formats:
- CLI: `repowise workspace impacted-tests backend-api:src/api/users.py`
- Table (human), JSON (machine), list (for piping to pytest)
- MCP tool: `get_workspace_test_impact(changed_files=[{"repo": "backend-api", "path": "src/api/users.py"}])`
- REST: `POST /api/workspace/test-impact`

## Alternatives Considered

1. **Manual per-repo runs** — what everyone does today. Slow, easy to miss a repo.
2. **Run full test suites everywhere** — wastes CI time, slow feedback.
3. **GitHub Actions matrix** — requires maintaining a separate workflow that duplicates logic Repowise already has.

## Additional Context

This completes the workspace intelligence matrix that the README documents:
- Contracts ✓
- Blast radius ✓  
- Breaking changes ✓
- **Test impact ← missing**

The underlying pieces already exist and are production-ready:
- Contract links (`contracts.py`) — provider↔consumer with confidence
- Test reachability (`test_reachability.py`) — 95.7% precision call-graph, 3-hop
- Test impact (`test_impact.py`) — unifies measured + inferred with basis tagging

This just joins them across repo boundaries. No new analysis engines needed, just cross-repo orchestration.

**Example workflow after this lands:**
```bash
# From workspace root
repowise workspace impacted-tests backend-api:src/api/users.py

# Output:
# Consumer: web-app (call-graph)
#   tests/api/users.test.ts (reaches users.py via UserService::getUser)
#   tests/integration/auth.test.ts (reaches users.py via AuthFlow)
#
# Consumer: mobile-app (import-graph)
#   tests/services/userService.test.ts (imports UserApi)
#
# Consumer: admin-panel (call-graph)
#   tests/api/adminUsers.test.ts (reaches users.py via AdminUserService)
#
# Total: 4 test files across 3 repos
```

records.title: Reject cyclic and invalid subscription parent relationships
records.body:
## Observed behavior

**Confirmed defect.** `Subscription.parent` permits self-parenting, cycles, cross-user relationships, and parenting beneath a non-folder subscription. Tree traversals do not track visited nodes, and the unread-list reduction loop has no no-progress exit.

## Expected behavior

Subscription relationships should form an acyclic tree owned by one user, with only folder subscriptions acting as parents. Traversal should terminate defensively even if legacy or externally written data violates those invariants.

## Reproduction and evidence

Create a folder subscription, then set its `parent` to itself. Calling `unread_count`, `get_unread_posts()`, `get_paginated_posts()`, `mark_read()`, or `get_unread_subscription_list_for_user()` can loop or recurse indefinitely.

Evidence: `feeds/models.py` lines 457-463 and 486-493; `feeds/utils.py` lines 479-495. No model validation or traversal visited set is present.

## Impact and risk

Malformed hierarchy data can hang application workers and scheduled jobs. Cross-user or non-folder parenting can also hide subscriptions or raise lookup errors. Existing records may already violate the intended invariants.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Self-parenting and ancestor cycles are rejected.
- [ ] A parent must be a folder subscription belonging to the same user.
- [ ] Traversal methods terminate safely when malformed legacy data exists.
- [ ] Tests cover self-cycles, multi-node cycles, cross-user parents, non-folder parents, and valid nested trees.

## Open questions

- Whether invalid legacy relationships should be detached, rejected by a data migration, or only guarded at runtime is unknown.

records.title: Extend sim/pll-lock and sim/vco measurement campaigns to the full PVT corner matrix
records.body:
## Original Issue

## Context

Issue #52 built `sim/harness/measure.py` (frequency/duty-cycle/lock-time
extraction from a transient trace) and two new measurement campaigns:

- `sim/pll-lock` — cold-start closed-loop lock measurement
  (`design/top/top.sch`, target 250 MHz = N=25 * 10 MHz Fref).
- `sim/vco` — frequency-vs-`VCTRL` characterization
  (`design/vco/vco_ring5.sch`, open loop).

Both manifests **declare** the full PVT grid this repo's other campaigns use
(`tt`/`ss`/`ff` x `-40`/`27`/`125` degC x `1.62`/`1.80`/`1.98` V), but the
first committed record for each is a **declared subset** (per
`sim/README.md`'s subset-justification rule), not the full grid:

- `sim/pll-lock/records/20260819-122135-fe0e6df.md` — 3 points only
  (`tt`/`ss`/`ff` @ 27 degC / 1.80 V nominal). Observed per-point cost:
  roughly 10-30 minutes of wall-clock ngspice simulation for a 3
  microsecond cold-start transient of the full closed-loop netlist, on the
  host that produced this record. `ff` timed out at this manifest's 1800 s
  per-point budget without finishing.
- `sim/vco/records/20260819-131741-fe0e6df.md` — 1 corner only (`tt` @ 27
  degC / 1.80 V nominal), 6 swept `VCTRL` values. Observed cost: roughly
  5-10 minutes of wall-clock simulation per swept `VCTRL` value.

At those per-point costs, the full 27-point grid is roughly 4.5-13.5 hours
of simulation for `sim/pll-lock` alone, and a comparable order for `sim/vco`
— clearly out of scope for the single session that produced the first
records.

## Scope

- [ ] Run `sim/pll-lock`'s full 27-point PVT grid (raise `--corners`/
      `--temps`/`--supply-tol` overrides, or just the bare manifest, with
      enough wall-clock budget — likely needs to run unattended over
      several hours, possibly split across multiple sessions/hosts). Write
      a new record that **supersedes**
      `sim/pll-lock/records/20260819-122135-fe0e6df.md`
      (`--supersedes 20260819-122135-fe0e6df`).
- [ ] Run `sim/vco`'s full 27-point PVT grid the same way, superseding
      `sim/vco/records/20260819-131741-fe0e6df.md`.
- [ ] If a per-point timeout still trips at some corners (like `ff` did in
      the first `sim/pll-lock` record), that is itself valid evidence to
      record, not a blocker — a manifest's `measure.timeout_s` may need
      raising if the true simulation cost (not a stuck/non-convergent run)
      is the cause; distinguish the two before raising it blindly.
- [ ] Consider whether the observed slow convergence (`Warning: singular
      matrix`, `Note: Starting dynamic gmin stepping` in several
      `sim/pll`/`sim/pll-lock` logs from issue #52) points at a harness/
      netlist issue (e.g. a missing/inconsistent initial condition) worth
      its own investigation, separate from just "give it more wall-clock
      budget" — file a separate issue if so; do not fold a design/harness
      fix into this issue's own scope.

## Non-goals

- No design/topology changes to any of the four PLL blocks.
- No spec ratification — this issue produces evidence only, same as #52.

## Related

- Issue #52 (the measurement-capability + first campaign issue this issue
  extends).
- `sim/harness/measure.py`'s module docstring (the lock/oscillation
  criteria applied).

---

## Curator Enhancement

<!-- loom:complexity=routine -->

### Dependencies

- [ ] PR #57 (`feat: add sim/harness measurement extraction + PLL lock/VCO campaigns`) must merge first.

**Why this blocks**: `sim/pll-lock/` and `sim/vco/` (the two campaigns this
issue extends to the full PVT grid) do not exist on `origin/main` as of
`5ee7c59` (2026-08-19) — they exist only on PR #57's branch. Verified: `git
ls-tree -r origin/main --name-only | grep -E '^sim/(pll-lock|vco)/'` returns
nothing.

PR #57 is fully code-reviewed and approved (Judge verdict posted
2026-08-19T14:06:21Z: "Code review: complete, no blocking issues found").
It is held out of the merge queue solely by an **org-level GitHub Actions
billing failure** unrelated to the diff (`loom:operator-only` +
`loom:operator-mechanical`), not by any outstanding review feedback. Once
billing is restored and PR #57 merges, this dependency clears automatically
and this issue can be unblocked per the "When Dependencies Complete" check.

### Verified corrections

- **2026-08-28, verified against `origin/main` @ `ca167f9`**: this issue's
  title and body repeatedly describe the target as "the full 27-point PVT
  grid" (`tt`/`ss`/`ff` × −40/27/125 °C × 1.62/1.80/1.98 V). That convention
  is now stale: `DR-003` (`spec/decision-records/DR-003-corner-and-temperature-scope.md`,

records.title: Spec: Stage 2.1 Part 2 — Material Ingestion & Pedagogical Concept Dependency GraphRAG
records.body:
# Spec: Stage 2.1 Part 2 — Material Ingestion & Pedagogical Concept Dependency GraphRAG (Rev. 2)

## Problem Statement

Learners uploading educational materials (lecture slides, textbook chapters, problem sets, and course notes) need an AI learning system that understands the strict hierarchical prerequisite structure of concepts rather than loose associative keyword links.

Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and macroscopic GraphRAG systems either treat documents as unorganized text chunks or build open-vocabulary associative co-occurrence graphs. These approaches fail in education because:

1. They cannot determine pedagogical learning order (e.g. whether *Limits* must be mastered before *Derivatives*), and even when they attempt to, they have no mechanism for separating a well-supported ordering from a single low-confidence guess.
2. They generate expensive, multi-turn community summaries and map-reduce retrieval loops (30,000–100,000+ tokens per query) with latency exceeding 15–30 seconds.
3. They fail to link concrete practice problems and past exam questions directly to conceptual prerequisites for targeted diagnostic remediation.
4. When two different course materials present conflicting curricular sequences, existing systems either crash with cycle deadlocks or silently corrupt the knowledge base without informing the learner — and even systems that avoid crashing rarely distinguish "one document briefly contradicted itself" from "two independent sources genuinely disagree," which is a very different signal.

## Solution

A deterministic, schema-constrained GraphRAG-Lite pipeline integrated directly into the unified single-app Next.js architecture (PostgreSQL + pgvector + Drizzle ORM, with zero external graph database dependencies).

During material ingestion, the system:

1. Batches multimodal extracted Markdown into structural, section-level payloads (strictly capped at ≤50,000 tokens per LLM pass to prevent lost-in-the-middle degradation), carrying forward a lightweight running concept registry across batches within the same material so later batches reuse existing slugs instead of re-inventing them.
2. Runs extraction in **two grounded passes** rather than one: Pass A extracts atomic Knowledge Components (KCs), PACER pedagogical classifications, Bloom taxonomy levels, and practice exercises per batch; Pass B — run after all of a material's batches complete Pass A — infers directional prerequisite dependencies using the *complete* material-wide concept list as grounding, on a model tier better suited to relational reasoning.
3. Sanitizes raw extraction output, dropping or flagging any edge or exercise link that references a concept id not present in the extracted concept set, before any graph algorithm touches the data.
4. Validates and enforces a clean Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) using a pure TypeScript integrity engine: Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components detection, an iterative confidence-and-corroboration-weighted Minimum Feedback Arc Set cycle-breaking loop, and Aho-Garey-Ullman transitive reduction.
5. Persists nodes to `knowledge_components` (with 768-dimensional dense vector embeddings), prerequisite edges to `knowledge_dependencies` (with an evidence log rather than a single opaque confidence float), and practice problems to `exercises` linked via `exercise_knowledge_components`.
6. Merges newly extracted concepts into a project-wide unified graph using deterministic slugification and vector cosine similarity deduplication, with a tiered policy that only auto-merges near-certain duplicates and routes ambiguous cases and cross-material pedagogical contradictions through the same interactive resolution surface — never silently, and never destructively.
7. Exposes sub-25ms SQL Recursive Common Table Expression (CTE) query interfaces and dual-output AI tools (`getGraphNeighborhood`, `getPrerequisiteChain`, `getExercisesForKc`) to empower the Goal Synthesis Bridge and Inner Loop Socratic Tutor.
8. Is continuously checked for extraction *accuracy* — not just structural validity — against a human-annotated golden set, so regressions in concept/edge extraction quality are caught the same way regressions in the deterministic algorithms are.

---

## User Stories

1. As a learner, I want my uploaded lecture slides and textbooks to be automatically analyzed for core Knowledge Components (KCs), so that I don't have to manually create study concept maps.
2. As a learner, I want each extracted Knowledge Component to have a clear PACER classification (Procedural, Analogous, Conceptual, Evidence, Reference), so that the system knows whether to test me with flashcards or deep diagnostic scenarios.
3. As a learner, I want the system to determine the exact cognitive depth (Bloom's taxonomy level) required for each concept, so that practice sessions challenge me at the appropriate level.
4. As a learner, I want the system to identify strict directional prerequisite relationships between concepts — including ones that span different sections or chapters of the same material — so that I am never asked to learn an advanced topic before mastering its foundations.
5. As a learner, I want practice exercises and exam problems from my materials to be extracted and linked to their target Knowledge Components, so that I can practice real test problems relevant to what I am studying.
6. As a learner, I want to see real-time progress indicators as my material progresses through chunking, embedding, concept extraction, dependency extraction, and DAG validation stages, so that I understand what the system is currently doing.
7. As a learner, I want materials with no conceptual knowledge (e.g. administrative course syllabus or title pages) to complete successfully without polluting my project knowledge graph, so that my curriculum remains clean.
8. As a learner, I want my concept graph to unify across multiple uploads (e.g. Lecture 1, Lecture 2, and textbook chapters) without duplicate n

records.title: package linking: propagate static-library native link requirements to final binaries
records.body:
# package linking: propagate static-library native link requirements to final binaries

## What problem does this solve?

The SPEC explicitly says a dependency `staticlib` package's `(link ...)`
section is not propagated. Only the final binary package's link section,
source `extern` metadata, CLI inputs, and dependency archives reach the linker.

A TypeLisp wrapper around SQLite, raylib, an OS library, or a vendored C archive
therefore cannot be consumed compositionally. Every downstream executable must
know the wrapper's private implementation dependencies and copy its libraries,
search paths, and raw arguments. Platform fixes must be repeated in every
binary and can fail only at the final link with a poor undefined-symbol
diagnostic.

## Describe the solution

Define native link requirements as part of a static-library package's public
runtime interface and propagate them across its direct root edge to the final
executable link plan. #6966 forbids that wrapper from owning normal TypeLisp
package dependencies, but explicitly permits its native `(link ...)` metadata.

At minimum, the existing all-target and Linux/Windows `(link ...)` fields on a
`staticlib` should describe consumer requirements. If TypeLisp needs both
private build inputs and exported consumer requirements once more artifact
kinds exist, give that distinction explicit manifest syntax rather than
guessing from usage.

Relative search paths must be resolved against the declaring dependency root,
not the root binary's working directory. Merge order and duplicate handling
must be deterministic and preserve static-linker ordering constraints; do not
globally sort or deduplicate values when that changes linker meaning. The final
runtime-input sidecar and machine-readable metadata must include the declaring
package and effective ordered link plan so freshness and diagnostics remain
explainable.

## Project-goal justification

Practical systems packages are frequently safe TypeLisp APIs over native
libraries. TypeLisp already treats FFI and native archives as core systems
features; forcing every binary to understand wrapper linker internals makes
those packages substantially less usable and less portable than their source
API suggests. This can be fixed and dogfooded under exact pins without waiting
for external users or a registry.

## Selfhost implementation target

- manifest link semantics and dependency graph nodes
- ordered link-plan construction and platform selection
- artifact freshness/runtime-input sidecars and package metadata
- linker diagnostics with requirement provenance
- local/remote dependency integration gates for Linux and Windows
- SPEC §4.6 and docs/packages.md

## Acceptance criteria

- A binary depending on a TypeLisp staticlib wrapper links and runs without
  repeating that wrapper's native libraries, search paths, or required args in
  the root manifest.
- Requirements from several directly declared wrappers merge exactly once
  where deduplication is semantics-preserving, including when two wrappers name
  the same system library or search path.
- Every relative search path is anchored to the manifest that declared it,
  including fetched cache roots and repository subdirectories from #6980,
  and follows proposal 34's checkout-containment rule.
- All-target and selected Linux/Windows requirements activate only in their
  documented contexts.
- Archive/library ordering supports mutual native static references;
  an adversarial fixture prevents an apparently deterministic but semantically
  wrong global sort/dedup implementation.
- A missing native library diagnostic identifies the dependency and manifest
  field that introduced it and shows a safely quoted effective search context.
- Any change to an active propagated input invalidates the final runtime
  artifact; inactive target inputs and TLCI-only state do not.
- `tree`/`metadata` or build-event output can explain the final ordered native
  link requirements once #6957/#6952 support is available.
- A remote dependency fixture covers cached/offline propagation, and Linux and
  Windows cover their native linker command shapes.

## Alternatives and non-goals

Requiring root binaries to redeclare everything is explicit but violates
encapsulation and does not scale. Automatically parsing undefined native
symbols cannot recover search paths, platform choices, ordering, or raw linker
requirements. This issue does not add build scripts, native source compilation,
shared libraries, C header generation, or system-library installation.

## Related work

Closed #1514, #1727, #2078-#2079, and #2892 established CLI, extern-owned, and
manifest native link inputs. Closed #1155/#1938 established the package archive
DAG. #6971 owns new C ABI artifact kinds. #6966 establishes the
dependency-free TypeLisp-library rule and its explicit C-wrapper exception;
this proposal supplies the direct library-to-binary native-link propagation
needed to make that exception usable.
